paper_meta.title: EEG-based upper alpha neurofeedback training improves working memory performance

hook_question: Can you train your brain to make more of one wave, and does it help you remember?

scenes.headline: EEG measures the brain's rhythms from the scalp
scenes.analogy_line: Like listening to a stadium crowd through the wall: you can't hear one voice, but you can hear the chant.
scenes.prose: Electrodes on the scalp pick up the summed activity of millions of neurons. The signal is sorted into frequency bands; upper alpha sits around 10 to 12 cycles per second.

claims.text: Upper alpha is a band around 10 to 12 Hz.

scenes.headline: Neurofeedback shows you a brain signal so you can learn to change it
scenes.analogy_line: Like a heart-rate monitor during a run, but for one brain rhythm.
scenes.prose: A participant watches a bar that tracks one feature of their own EEG and tries to move it. Over sessions the brain can learn to produce more of that feature.

scenes.headline: Nobody knew whether raising upper alpha would improve memory
scenes.prose: Earlier work had linked upper alpha to working memory, but correlation is not training. The open question was whether pushing the rhythm up would move memory with it.

claims.text: Prior studies linked upper alpha to working memory performance.

scenes.headline: Feedback appeared only when upper-alpha power crossed a threshold
scenes.analogy_line: Like a thermostat that only clicks on above a set point.
scenes.prose: Participants received visual feedback whenever their upper alpha amplitude exceeded an individually determined threshold, over five training sessions. A control group received feedback tied to nothing.

claims.text: Feedback was given when upper alpha amplitude exceeded an individual threshold.
The thermostat comparison is an analogy, not the paper's description.

scenes.headline: After five sessions, what happened to working memory?
scenes.analogy_line: Lock in a guess before the paper answers.
scenes.prediction_question: After five sessions of upper-alpha training, what happened to working memory?
prediction_options: Alpha rose and working memory improved
Alpha rose but working memory did not change

scenes.headline: Alpha went up, and so did working memory
scenes.prose: The trained group raised their upper-alpha power across sessions, and their working-memory scores rose with it. The sham group moved on neither.

claims.text: Working memory improved in the neurofeedback group compared with the control group.

scenes.reveal_note: Both rose, and only in the trained group.

scenes.headline: A trainable rhythm became a candidate memory intervention
scenes.prose: The result made upper-alpha training a plausible tool rather than a correlation, and set up later work on who responds and how long it lasts.

claims.text: The authors propose upper-alpha training as a way to enhance cognitive performance.

widgets.task_question: What happens to learning if the reward threshold is set too high?

nudges.name: threshold
nudges.text: too high and nobody gets rewarded; learning stalls

concepts.name: EEG
concepts.one_line: Scalp recording of summed neural rhythms.

concepts.name: Neurofeedback
concepts.one_line: Seeing a brain signal so you can learn to change it.

concepts.name: Reward threshold
concepts.one_line: The level a signal must cross before feedback rewards it.
